title: Creating Anglo-America
summary: After the Restoration of 1660, England expanded its American empire under mercantilist principles, passing Navigation Acts to channel colonial trade through English ships and ports. New colonies multiplied: New Netherland was seized in 1664 and renamed New York, Carolina was founded as a Barbados offshoot that would build a rice-and-slave economy, and William Penn launched Pennsylvania in 1681 as a Quaker 'holy experiment' offering religious liberty, cheap land, and initially fair dealings with Indians. English-Iroquois cooperation was formalized in the Covenant Chain, though alliances shifted as imperial rivalries evolved.

The late seventeenth century brought cascading crises. King Philip's War (1675-1676) devastated New England but broke Indian power there, and Bacon's Rebellion (1676) revealed the dangers of a discontented class of landless former servants in Virginia, accelerating the shift from indentured servitude to African slavery. Lawmakers hardened racial lines: hereditary status followed the mother, conversion no longer freed slaves, and the 1705 Virginia slave code turned the colony into a full slave society. England's Glorious Revolution of 1688 echoed in America through the collapse of the Dominion of New England, Leisler's Rebellion in New York, and Maryland's Protestant uprising, while a new Massachusetts charter and the Salem witch trials of 1692 marked the transformation of the Puritan commonwealth.

The eighteenth century then brought stability and dramatic growth. The mainland population increased nearly tenfold between 1700 and 1770, swelled by German, Scotch-Irish, convict, and enslaved African migrants who made the colonies strikingly diverse in ethnicity and religion. Regions diverged, from New England towns to the grain-exporting Middle Colonies, plantation South, and fast-growing backcountry, while a consumer revolution and Atlantic commerce tied colonists to Britain. An Anglicized elite of merchants and planters dominated society above a broad middle rank of landowning farmers, growing numbers of poor, and enslaved people, as expanding settlement steadily eroded Indian land and autonomy, as in the fraudulent Walking Purchase of 1737.
big_ideas: Mercantilism and the Navigation Acts organized the empire so colonial trade would enrich England, while lax enforcement let colonists prosper within the system.
Restoration-era colonies, New York, Carolina, and Pennsylvania, expanded English America with very different visions, from feudal hierarchy to Quaker religious liberty.
Bacon's Rebellion exposed class conflict among whites and pushed Chesapeake planters to replace indentured servants with enslaved Africans.
Slavery was constructed gradually through law, and by the early 1700s Virginia had become a slave society with race as its central social divide.
The Glorious Revolution triggered colonial uprisings and entrenched the ideology of English liberty, parliamentary supremacy, and Protestant identity.
Massive eighteenth-century immigration from Germany, Ireland, Scotland, and Africa created an ethnically and religiously diverse population unlike England's.
Colonial society grew more stratified even as most free families owned land, and elites increasingly modeled themselves on the English gentry through Anglicization.

key_terms.def: Economic doctrine holding that governments should regulate trade so exports exceeded imports and colonies enriched the mother country by supplying raw materials and buying its manufactures.
Parliamentary laws beginning in 1651 requiring that key 'enumerated' colonial goods like tobacco and sugar travel in English ships through English ports, aimed at breaking Dutch commercial dominance.
1675-1676 Indian uprising in New England led in colonial eyes by the Wampanoag leader Metacom; its defeat opened land to settlers while permanently breaking the region's Indian power.
Alliance formed in the 1670s between New York's governor Edmund Andros and the Iroquois in which English and Iroquois ambitions reinforced each other before the Iroquois turned to neutrality.

1676 Virginia revolt in which Nathaniel Bacon rallied small farmers, servants, and landless men against Governor Berkeley's Indian policy and corrupt rule; it frightened elites into relying more on enslaved labor.
Quaker proprietor who founded Pennsylvania in 1681 as a 'holy experiment' committed to religious freedom, an elected assembly, and purchasing land from Indians rather than seizing it.
Religious movement teaching that God's 'inner light' dwells in every person; Quakers embraced spiritual equality, pacifism, and eventually became early opponents of slavery.
1688 overthrow of the Catholic James II in favor of William and Mary, which confirmed parliamentary supremacy and the idea that liberty was every Englishman's birthright.
1689 enactment listing Parliament's powers, such as control of taxation, and individual protections like trial by jury, justifying James II's removal and defining English liberty.
James II's 1686-1689 consolidation of the New England colonies plus New York and the Jerseys under Sir Edmund Andros without an elected assembly; colonists dismantled it when James fell.
1689 seizure of power in New York by militia captain Jacob Leisler after the Glorious Revolution; his execution polarized the colony's politics for a generation.
1692 wave of witchcraft accusations in Massachusetts that led to nineteen hangings before the governor halted the proceedings, discrediting witch prosecutions in America.
Comprehensive law defining enslaved people as property fully subject to their owners, separating black and white courts, and marking Virginia's completed transition to a slave society.
Indentured families, many German, who received Atlantic passage in exchange for a promise to work off the cost after arrival, a key mechanism of eighteenth-century immigration.
1737 Pennsylvania land fraud in which hired runners, rather than a walking man, marked off a cession from the Lenni Lenape, poisoning the colony's once-peaceful Indian relations.
Rapidly growing inland region from central Pennsylvania down the Shenandoah Valley into the upland Carolinas, settled largely by Scotch-Irish and German farm families.

timeline.event: Parliament passes the first Navigation Act to control colonial commerce.
England seizes New Netherland from the Dutch and renames it New York.
The first settlers, many from Barbados, arrive in Carolina.
King Philip's War erupts in New England, devastating both settlers and Indians.
Bacon's Rebellion burns Jamestown and shakes Virginia's ruling elite.
William Penn receives the charter for Pennsylvania, his Quaker 'holy experiment.'
James II merges the northern colonies into the Dominion of New England under Edmund Andros.
The Glorious Revolution replaces James II with William and Mary.
Colonial uprisings topple Andros in Boston, Leisler takes New York, and Maryland Protestants oust the proprietor; Parliament enacts the Bill of Rights.
The Salem witch trials result in nineteen executions in Massachusetts.
Virginia adopts a sweeping slave code defining enslaved people as property.
The Walking Purchase defrauds the Lenni Lenape of Pennsylvania land.

themes: Politics and power: The Glorious Revolution and colonial rebellions spread the ideology of English liberty while Britain tried, unevenly, to tighten imperial control.
Work, exchange, and technology: Mercantilist trade laws, the rise of staple crop plantations, and a transatlantic consumer revolution bound colonial economies to the Atlantic world.
Migration and settlement: German, Scotch-Irish, convict, and enslaved African arrivals diversified the colonies and pushed settlement into the backcountry at Indians' expense.
American and regional identity: Distinct regional societies emerged even as elites pursued Anglicization, and race hardened into the key line dividing freedom from slavery.
Social structures: Law converted slavery into a hereditary, racial institution, while free society stratified into gentry, a broad landowning middle, and a growing poor.
